The paper attempts to fill this gap by making an initial attempt to illustrate the relevance of this vital distinction in this area. Following the discussion of some crucial preliminary issues, the two types of knowledge are characterized and challenges involved in their measurement are considered. Subsequently, the distinction is related to theoretical accounts of how L2 pronunciation is learnt and empirical investigations into the effectiveness of different types of pronunciation instruction as well as everyday instructional classroom practices. The role of mediating factors, such as individual differences or contextual influences, is also considered. 1 INTRODUCTION While learning accurate second or foreign language (L2) pronunciation may not always be seen as first priority, with teachers often being advised to focus on comprehensibility and intelligibility (Levis, 2018), the role of this target language (TL) subsystem depends on the objectives of a particular course or program. For obvious reasons, good, perhaps even native-like, mastery of pronunciation will be an important goal for students enrolled in degree programs in an additional language who aspire to become experts when it comes to TL use. By contrast, in L2 instruction in elementary or secondary school, pronunciation is often pushed to the sidelines because of limited time and the need to achieve other important curricular goals which, of course, are bound to vary from one educational context to the next. It should be kept in mind, however, that comprehensibility and intelligibility will be impossible to attain if learners are not at least to some extent aware of pronunciation features and are able to use these features in different situations. For example, failing to deliver word or sentence stress properly can result in a diminished ability to successfully get messages across. This indicates that L2 pronunciation deserves some degree of attention, irrespective of the nature of a given L2 course or program. Learning L2 pronunciation, however, is no easy feat if we consider the fact that there may exist a sensitive period for successful acquisition of this TL subsystem (Granena & Long, 2012). Even though individual differences, such as aptitude, motivation, willingness to communicate, adept use of language learning strategies, or group identification, may ameliorate the detrimental effect of age to some extent (Hansen-Edwards, 2018), there is no denying that many learners struggle with their L2 pronunciation, even if the modest goal of intelligibility is pursued (Levis, 2005). In addition, the effects of classroom instruction may, in many cases, fall short of the expectations of teachers and learners. In particular, while intensive practice is likely to help many students to produce and perceive specific sounds, stress patterns, or intonation contours when they pay deliberate attention to such features, this apparent control tends to disappear in spontaneous interactions under time pressure when attentional resources are allocated to competing processes (Kormos, 2006). This brings us to the crucial distinction between explicit and implicit knowledge that has been at the core of second language acquisition (SLA) theory and research for several decades (DeKeyser, 2017; Ellis, 2009a; Ellis & Roever, 2018; Godfroid, 2022a; Pawlak, 2019, 2021a, 2021b). This assessment also applies to the mastery of pronunciation. This is because although the role of explicit and implicit representation may have been indirectly implied in some theoretical accounts of how L2 pronunciation is learned (e.g., Major, 2008), it has been marginally recognized in empirical studies (cf. Saito, 2021), including recent, related work on phonological vocabulary knowledge (e.g., Saito et al., 2023; Uchihara et al., 2024). Surpris- ingly, research on these strategies is scarce, mainly focusing on the identifica- tion and classification of PLS, diverse instruments are used for data collection and the findings are inconclusive. The paper provides an overview of the avail- able research on PLS with respect to their identification, learners' preferences concerning their use, factors mediating the application of PLS, and the effects of strategies-based instruction in this area. An attempt is also made to assess research of this kind and to suggest how it could be taken forward to provide insights that would be of value to practitioners. Consequently, stu- dents who wish to improve their pronunciation, whatever their individual goals might be, usually have to do this in their own time, which clearly calls for the ability to set realistic goals, choose appropriate ways of learning, engage in con- stant monitoring and conduct valid self-evaluation. Since adept use of language learning strategies (LLS) is seen by many specialists as a vital, or perhaps even in- dispensable condition for the development of autonomy in L2 learning (e.g., Grif- fiths, 2013; Oxford, 1990, 2011, 2017; Wenden, 1991), it can reasonably be ar- gued that the same applies to learning TL pronunciation. The aim of this paper is to remedy this situation by providing an exhaustive overview of the existing studies of PLS, making an at- tempt to critically evaluate such research in terms of its focus and methodology, and suggesting ways in which this line of inquiry can be beneficially moved for- ward. Pronunciation learning strategies are usually characterized in the literature as combinations of deliberate action, awareness, and internal regulation, with explicit and implicit distinctions central to understanding whether a strategy is consciously used or automatically executed. The evidence points to a broad framework in which “explicit” learning refers to awareness and conscious engagement, while “implicit” learning refers to acquisition through natural, less consciously monitored processes [N1-R4]. In pronunciation instruction, this distinction is especially important because mastery of pronunciation often requires both explicit awareness of features and the eventual automatic use of those features in production [N4-F1].

A key way to interpret strategy awareness is that explicit strategies are those learners consciously employ, often in a logical sequence, with the purpose of improving pronunciation control [N4-F2]. This aligns with the broader language-learning-strategies literature, where successful learners tend to apply strategies in an orchestrated way that is relevant to their own needs and task characteristics [N3-R2]. By contrast, implicitly automatic strategies are those that become habitual or unconscious, such as routine pronunciation adjustments that learners make without deliberate reflection [N1-R1]. The literature on implicit learning also emphasizes that implicit knowledge is acquired naturally, often without metalinguistic awareness, whereas explicit learning is defined as learning with that awareness [N1-R4].

Intentionality differs across strategy types because some strategies are self-directed and metacognitive, while others may become habit-based or less intentional. Self-monitoring is a metacognitive process in which learners direct attention to enhance awareness of their cognitive and behavioral functioning, which makes it a highly intentional strategy [N5-R2]. In pronunciation learning, self-monitoring can be overtly practiced, such as when learners deliberately check their own production or adjust their articulation [N2-R1]. Habit-based practice, by contrast, is often less intentional and more automatic, relying on repeated exposure and internalized routines rather than conscious planning [N1-R1]. This distinction matters because intentionality shapes how learners select and use strategies: explicit strategies are typically chosen and monitored, while implicit strategies may be used without conscious awareness [N1-R4].

Metacognitive awareness plays a central role in strategy selection and use. Metacognition is defined as awareness and regulation of one’s own learning process, and it is a cornerstone of effective language learning [N5-F3]. In the context of pronunciation, this means learners who have stronger metacognitive awareness are better able to choose appropriate strategies, evaluate their effectiveness, and adjust their approach when needed [N5-F3]. The evidence also suggests that metacognitive instruction can enhance comprehension and self-regulated learning, which implies that learners with better metacognitive awareness are more likely to engage in deliberate, strategic pronunciation work [N5-R1]. This supports the view that metacognitive awareness is not just a side effect of strategy use, but a prerequisite for intentional strategy selection [N5-F3].

Overall, pronunciation learning strategies are best understood as a spectrum from explicitly aware, intentionality-rich strategies to implicitly automatic, less consciously monitored strategies [N1-R4][N4-F2]. Awareness and intentionality are therefore not binary attributes; they vary across strategies and over time as learners develop mastery [N3-R2][N4-F1].

Pronunciation learning actions can be both overt and covert, depending on whether they are directly observable or rely on internal processing. The evidence indicates that overt actions are those that learners perform visibly and can be observed by others, such as repeated practice, deliberate production attempts, or self-monitoring behaviors [N2-R1][N4-F2]. These actions are often associated with strategy implementation because they represent the visible application of a strategy, such as practicing a difficult word multiple times or adjusting pronunciation after feedback [N2-R3][N2-R5]. The literature also notes that pronunciation learning strategies can include both observable and unobservable actions, with observable examples being “numerous repetitions of words that are difficult to pronounce” and unobservable examples being “a mental plan of how to get around a persistent pronunciation problem” [N4-F2]. This operationalization is important because it shows that researchers distinguish between behavior that is visible and behavior that is internalized.

Covert actions, by contrast, rely on internal processing and are not directly observable. They include mental planning, self-monitoring, and the internal regulation of learning behavior that supports strategy use [N5-R2][N4-F2]. The evidence on self-monitoring suggests that this process involves directing attention and enhancing metacognitive awareness, which can be internal rather than external [N5-R2]. In pronunciation learning, covert actions are especially relevant for strategies that become habit-based or automatic, because they reflect the internal mechanisms that underlie production and self-adjustment [N1-R1]. The literature also notes that implicit prosody cannot be observed directly, but can be inferred through self-reports, which further underscores the distinction between observable and non-observable features [N4-R5].

Observable actions are closely tied to strategy implementation and feedback because they provide a direct basis for evaluation and improvement. When learners repeat words, practice pronunciation aloud, or receive feedback on their production, the overt nature of those actions makes them easier to assess and modify [N2-R3][N2-R5]. The strategy-based model for pronunciation instruction emphasized in the evidence also suggests that observable strategy use can be the target of instruction, because learners can be taught to employ specific steps or chains of actions that improve pronunciation learning [N2-R2][N4-F2]. However, the same evidence also notes that some actions, such as mental plans, are less directly observable and may therefore be harder to measure or observe in real time [N4-F2].

In short, pronunciation learning actions are characterized as a mix of overt and covert behaviors. Overt actions are directly observable and often serve as the visible manifestation of strategy use, while covert actions depend on internal processing and are less easily observed [N2-R1][N4-F2]. Observable actions are especially important for feedback and strategy implementation, whereas covert actions support the underlying control and adjustment needed for effective pronunciation learning [N5-R2][N4-R5].

In summary, pronunciation learning strategies are characterized as a combination of awareness, intentionality, and observability. Explicit strategies are consciously aware and intentional, often involving self-monitoring and deliberate practice [N1-R4][N5-R2][N4-F2]. Implicit strategies are automatic and habit-based, often relying on internal processing rather than conscious attention [N1-R1][N4-F1]. Actions can be overt and directly observable, such as repeated practice and visible self-monitoring, or covert and less directly observable, such as mental planning and implicit prosody [N2-R1][N4-F2][N4-R5]. Metacognitive awareness supports strategy selection and use, while explicit instruction can make strategy use more observable and transferable [N5-F3][N4-F1][N6-R5]. Overall, pronunciation learning strategies are best understood as a spectrum from intentional, conscious action to automatic, less directly observable behavior, with explicit and implicit knowledge playing a complementary role in mastery [N1-R4][N4-F1][N4-F2].

Pronunciation learning strategies are usually characterized in the literature as combinations of deliberate action, awareness, and internal regulation, with explicit and implicit distinctions central to understanding whether a strategy is consciously used or automatically executed. The evidence points to a broad framework in which “explicit” learning refers to awareness and conscious engagement, while “implicit” learning refers to acquisition through natural, less consciously monitored processes [N1-R4]. In pronunciation instruction, this distinction is especially important because mastery of pronunciation often requires both explicit awareness of features and the eventual automatic use of those features in production [N4-F1].

A key way to interpret strategy awareness is that explicit strategies are those learners consciously employ, often in a logical sequence, with the purpose of improving pronunciation control [N4-F2]. This aligns with the broader language-learning-strategies literature, where successful learners tend to apply strategies in an orchestrated way that is relevant to their own needs and task characteristics [N3-R2]. By contrast, implicitly automatic strategies are those that become habitual or unconscious, such as routine pronunciation adjustments that learners make without deliberate reflection [N1-R1]. The literature on implicit learning also emphasizes that implicit knowledge is acquired naturally, often without metalinguistic awareness, whereas explicit learning is defined as learning with that awareness [N1-R4].

Intentionality differs across strategy types because some strategies are self-directed and metacognitive, while others may become habit-based or less intentional. Self-monitoring is a metacognitive process in which learners direct attention to enhance awareness of their cognitive and behavioral functioning, which makes it a highly intentional strategy [N5-R2]. In pronunciation learning, self-monitoring can be overtly practiced, such as when learners deliberately check their own production or adjust their articulation [N2-R1]. Habit-based practice, by contrast, is often less intentional and more automatic, relying on repeated exposure and internalized routines rather than conscious planning [N1-R1]. This distinction matters because intentionality shapes how learners select and use strategies: explicit strategies are typically chosen and monitored, while implicit strategies may be used without conscious awareness [N1-R4].

Metacognitive awareness plays a central role in strategy selection and use. Metacognition is defined as awareness and regulation of one’s own learning process, and it is a cornerstone of effective language learning [N5-F3]. In the context of pronunciation, this means learners who have stronger metacognitive awareness are better able to choose appropriate strategies, evaluate their effectiveness, and adjust their approach when needed [N5-F3]. The evidence also suggests that metacognitive instruction can enhance comprehension and self-regulated learning, which implies that learners with better metacognitive awareness are more likely to engage in deliberate, strategic pronunciation work [N5-R1]. This supports the view that metacognitive awareness is not just a side effect of strategy use, but a prerequisite for intentional strategy selection [N5-F3].

Overall, pronunciation learning strategies are best understood as a spectrum from explicitly aware, intentionality-rich strategies to implicitly automatic, less consciously monitored strategies [N1-R4][N4-F2]. Awareness and intentionality are therefore not binary attributes; they vary across strategies and over time as learners develop mastery [N3-R2][N4-F1].

Pronunciation learning actions can be both overt and covert, depending on whether they are directly observable or rely on internal processing. The evidence indicates that overt actions are those that learners perform visibly and can be observed by others, such as repeated practice, deliberate production attempts, or self-monitoring behaviors [N2-R1][N4-F2]. These actions are often associated with strategy implementation because they represent the visible application of a strategy, such as practicing a difficult word multiple times or adjusting pronunciation after feedback [N2-R3][N2-R5]. The literature also notes that pronunciation learning strategies can include both observable and unobservable actions, with observable examples being “numerous repetitions of words that are difficult to pronounce” and unobservable examples being “a mental plan of how to get around a persistent pronunciation problem” [N4-F2]. This operationalization is important because it shows that researchers distinguish between behavior that is visible and behavior that is internalized.

Covert actions, by contrast, rely on internal processing and are not directly observable. They include mental planning, self-monitoring, and the internal regulation of learning behavior that supports strategy use [N5-R2][N4-F2]. The evidence on self-monitoring suggests that this process involves directing attention and enhancing metacognitive awareness, which can be internal rather than external [N5-R2]. In pronunciation learning, covert actions are especially relevant for strategies that become habit-based or automatic, because they reflect the internal mechanisms that underlie production and self-adjustment [N1-R1]. The literature also notes that implicit prosody cannot be observed directly, but can be inferred through self-reports, which further underscores the distinction between observable and non-observable features [N4-R5].

Observable actions are closely tied to strategy implementation and feedback because they provide a direct basis for evaluation and improvement. When learners repeat words, practice pronunciation aloud, or receive feedback on their production, the overt nature of those actions makes them easier to assess and modify [N2-R3][N2-R5]. The strategy-based model for pronunciation instruction emphasized in the evidence also suggests that observable strategy use can be the target of instruction, because learners can be taught to employ specific steps or chains of actions that improve pronunciation learning [N2-R2][N4-F2]. However, the same evidence also notes that some actions, such as mental plans, are less directly observable and may therefore be harder to measure or observe in real time [N4-F2].

In short, pronunciation learning actions are characterized as a mix of overt and covert behaviors. Overt actions are directly observable and often serve as the visible manifestation of strategy use, while covert actions depend on internal processing and are less easily observed [N2-R1][N4-F2]. Observable actions are especially important for feedback and strategy implementation, whereas covert actions support the underlying control and adjustment needed for effective pronunciation learning [N5-R2][N4-R5].

Explicit knowledge refers to knowledge that learners are aware of and can verbalize, while implicit knowledge refers to knowledge that is acquired through repeated exposure and becomes automatic, often without conscious awareness [N4-F1][N1-R4]. The evidence on explicit and implicit knowledge of second language pronunciation explicitly states that the distinction is crucial to understanding L2 pronunciation learning and that it has been mainly applied to grammar, with pronunciation largely neglected in empirical studies [N4-F1]. This implies that pronunciation mastery depends on both explicit awareness and implicit automaticity, with the former enabling deliberate control and the latter enabling fluent, spontaneous production [N4-F1].

Mastery relates to conscious awareness and automaticity in a complementary way. The evidence indicates that comprehensibility and intelligibility depend on learners being at least somewhat aware of pronunciation features and able to use them in different situations [N4-F1]. This means that mastery is not simply about producing sounds correctly, but about being able to use pronunciation features intentionally and automatically across contexts. The literature also notes that controlled use of pronunciation tends to disappear in spontaneous interactions under time pressure, suggesting that automaticity is necessary for effective performance in real communication [N4-F1]. At the same time, explicit instruction is often needed to develop awareness and controlled use before those skills can become automatic [N4-F1].

Explicit instruction affects observable versus covert strategy use by increasing the likelihood that learners will engage in deliberate, observable strategies. The evidence on explicit and implicit knowledge emphasizes that explicit learning is defined as learning with metalinguistic awareness, while implicit learning is learning without that awareness [N1-R4]. In pronunciation learning, this means that explicit instruction can lead to observable practice, repetition, and self-monitoring behaviors, whereas implicit instruction may lead to more covert, habitual use of pronunciation patterns [N4-F1]. The literature also suggests that explicit instruction is more effective than implicit instruction for teaching spelling rules when generalization is aimed at, which supports the idea that explicit instruction can make strategy use more visible and transferable [N6-R5]. ## Integrated answer on how pronunciation learning strategies are characterized in terms of awareness, intentionality, and observability

Pronunciation learning strategies are best understood as intentional, awareness-based processes that can be both observable and covert, depending on how they are implemented. Across the branch reports, the literature consistently frames these strategies in terms of explicit and implicit learning, conscious awareness, and observable versus internalized behavior. The core distinction is that explicit strategies are deliberately used with awareness, while implicit strategies become habitual or automatic, often without conscious attention [N1-R4][N4-F1][N4-F2]. This creates a spectrum from intentionally planned, observable action to internally regulated, less directly observable execution.

### Awareness and intentionality

Awareness is central to how pronunciation learning strategies are characterized. The evidence shows that explicit learning is defined as learning with metalinguistic awareness, whereas implicit learning is learning without that awareness [N1-R4]. In pronunciation instruction, this means learners may consciously engage in strategies such as self-monitoring, deliberate practice, or strategy planning, or they may use pronunciation features automatically without conscious attention [N1-R1][N4-F2]. 

Intentionality differs across strategy types. Self-monitoring is a highly intentional metacognitive process in which learners direct attention to enhance awareness of their cognitive and behavioral functioning [N5-R2]. In pronunciation learning, this can manifest as learners checking their own production, adjusting articulation, or reflecting on how they sound [N2-R1][N5-F3]. By contrast, habit-based practice is often less intentional and more automatic, relying on repeated exposure and internalized routines rather than conscious planning [N1-R1][N4-F2]. This matters because intentionality shapes how learners select and use strategies: explicit strategies are typically chosen and monitored, while implicit strategies may be used without conscious awareness [N1-R4].

Metacognitive awareness also plays a central role in strategy selection and use. Metacognition is defined as awareness and regulation of one’s own learning process, and it is a cornerstone of effective language learning [N5-F3]. In pronunciation learning, this means learners with stronger metacognitive awareness are better able to choose appropriate strategies, evaluate their effectiveness, and adjust their approach when needed [N5-F3]. The evidence also suggests that metacognitive instruction can enhance comprehension and self-regulated learning, which implies that learners with better metacognitive awareness are more likely to engage in deliberate, strategic pronunciation work [N5-R1]. In short, metacognitive awareness is not just a side effect of strategy use; it is a prerequisite for intentional strategy selection [N5-F3].

### Observability of pronunciation learning actions

Pronunciation learning actions can be both overt and covert. Overt actions are directly observable and often serve as the visible manifestation of strategy use, such as repeated pronunciation practice, deliberate production attempts, or visible self-monitoring behaviors [N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-F2]. These actions are important because they provide a direct basis for evaluation and improvement [N2-R3][N2-R5]. The literature also notes that pronunciation learning strategies can include both observable and unobservable actions, with observable examples being “numerous repetitions of words that are difficult to pronounce” and unobservable examples being “a mental plan of how to get around a persistent pronunciation problem” [N4-F2]. This operationalization is important because it shows that researchers distinguish between behavior that is visible and behavior that is internalized.

Covert actions rely on internal processing and are less directly observable. They include mental planning, self-monitoring, and the internal regulation of learning behavior that supports strategy use [N5-R2][N4-F2]. The evidence on implicit prosody is especially useful for operationalizing non-observable features, because it notes that implicit prosody cannot be observed directly, but can be inferred through self-reports [N4-R5]. This suggests that researchers often rely on a combination of direct observation and indirect measures when assessing pronunciation strategy use [N4-R5].

Observable actions are especially important for strategy implementation and feedback. When learners repeat words, practice pronunciation aloud, or receive feedback on their production, the overt nature of those actions makes them easier to assess and modify [N2-R3][N2-R5]. The strategy-based model for pronunciation instruction emphasized in the evidence also suggests that observable strategy use can be the target of instruction, because learners can be taught to employ specific steps or chains of actions that improve pronunciation learning [N2-R2][N4-F2]. However, the same evidence also notes that some actions, such as mental plans, are less directly observable and may therefore be harder to measure or observe in real time [N4-F2].

### Explicit vs. implicit knowledge and pronunciation strategy implementation

Explicit knowledge and implicit knowledge differ in pronunciation in terms of conscious awareness and automatic execution. Explicit knowledge refers to knowledge that learners are aware of and can verbalize, while implicit knowledge refers to knowledge that is acquired through repeated exposure and becomes automatic, often without conscious awareness [N4-F1][N1-R4]. The evidence on explicit and implicit knowledge of second language pronunciation explicitly states that the distinction is crucial to understanding L2 pronunciation learning and that it has been mainly applied to grammar, with pronunciation largely neglected in empirical studies [N4-F1]. This implies that pronunciation mastery depends on both explicit awareness and implicit automaticity, with the former enabling deliberate control and the latter enabling fluent, spontaneous production [N4-F1].

Mastery relates to conscious awareness and automaticity in a complementary way. The evidence indicates that comprehensibility and intelligibility depend on learners being at least somewhat aware of pronunciation features and able to use them in different situations [N4-F1]. This means that mastery is not simply about producing sounds correctly, but about being able to use pronunciation features intentionally and automatically across contexts. The literature also notes that controlled use of pronunciation tends to disappear in spontaneous interactions under time pressure, suggesting that automaticity is necessary for effective performance in real communication [N4-F1]. At the same time, explicit instruction is often needed to develop awareness and controlled use before those skills can become automatic [N4-F1].

Explicit instruction affects observable versus covert strategy use by increasing the likelihood that learners will engage in deliberate, observable strategies. The evidence on explicit and implicit knowledge emphasizes that explicit learning is defined as learning with metalinguistic awareness, while implicit learning is learning without that awareness [N1-R4]. In pronunciation learning, this means that explicit instruction can lead to observable practice, repetition, and self-monitoring behaviors, whereas implicit instruction may lead to more covert, habitual use of pronunciation patterns [N4-F1]. The literature also suggests that explicit instruction is more effective than implicit instruction for teaching spelling rules when generalization is aimed at, which supports the idea that explicit instruction can make strategy use more visible and transferable [N6-R5]. However, the evidence also notes that implicit prosody cannot be observed directly, indicating that not all strategy use is overt [N4-R5].

### Typologies and terminology used in the literature

The literature on pronunciation learning strategies uses several common typologies and terminology, particularly explicit vs. implicit, conscious vs. unconscious, and strategy use vs. strategy knowledge. The most direct terminology in the evidence is “explicit” and “implicit,” with explicit learning defined as learning with metalinguistic awareness and implicit learning defined as learning without that awareness [N1-R4]. Another related distinction is “conscious” vs. “unconscious” or “automatic,” which appears in the broader language-learning-strategies literature as a way to describe how learners engage with strategies [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The evidence also notes that learners may use strategies consciously or habitually, with some actions being observable and others being internalized or unobservable [N4-F2].

Authors distinguish strategy use from strategy knowledge by treating strategy use as the actual application of a strategy, while strategy knowledge refers to the awareness or understanding that supports that use. In the context of pronunciation, this distinction is important because learners may know something about pronunciation features or strategies without necessarily using them deliberately [N4-F1]. The Oxford literature on language learning strategies is especially relevant here, because it emphasizes that successful learners apply strategies in an orchestrated way that is relevant to their own needs and task characteristics, implying that strategy knowledge is not the same as strategy use [N3-R2]. The evidence also shows that metacognitive awareness is central to strategy use, because it allows learners to monitor, modify, and regulate their learning behavior [N5-F3].

Observable vs. non-observable features are operationalized in studies in different ways. Some studies treat observable actions as those that can be directly recorded or observed, such as repeated pronunciation practice, self-monitoring behaviors, or visible production attempts [N2-R1][N2-R3]. Other studies recognize that not all strategy use is visible, and therefore distinguish between observable and unobservable actions, such as mental planning versus overt repetition [N4-F2]. The literature on implicit prosody is especially useful for operationalizing non-observable features, because it notes that implicit prosody cannot be observed directly but can be inferred through self-reports [N4-R5]. This suggests that researchers often rely on a combination of direct observation and indirect measures when assessing pronunciation strategy use.

In addition to explicit/implicit and conscious/unconscious distinctions, the literature also uses categories such as cognitive, metacognitive, and social strategies to classify pronunciation learning strategies [N4-R3]. This classification helps authors operationalize strategy use by separating strategies that directly support pronunciation learning from those that indirectly support the learning process [N3-R5]. The evidence also shows that pronunciation learning strategies can be clustered into chains or sequences, which implies that strategy use is often not a single isolated action, but a coordinated set of deliberate steps [N4-F2]. Taken together, these typologies and terminology reflect a broader effort to characterize pronunciation learning as a dynamic interplay between awareness, intentionality, and observable behavior [N3-R1][N4-F2][N5-F3].

## Conclusion

In summary, pronunciation learning strategies are characterized as a combination of awareness, intentionality, and observability. Explicit strategies are consciously aware and intentional, often involving self-monitoring and deliberate practice [N1-R4][N5-R2][N4-F2]. Implicit strategies are automatic and habit-based, often relying on internal processing rather than conscious attention [N1-R1][N4-F1]. Actions can be overt and directly observable, such as repeated practice and visible self-monitoring, or covert and less directly observable, such as mental planning and implicit prosody [N2-R1][N4-F2][N4-R5]. Metacognitive awareness supports strategy selection and use, while explicit instruction can make strategy use more observable and transferable [N5-F3][N4-F1][N6-R5]. Overall, pronunciation learning strategies are best understood as a spectrum from intentional, conscious action to automatic, less directly observable behavior, with explicit and implicit knowledge playing a complementary role in mastery [N1-R4][N4-F1][N4-F2].
